subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the UK, monetary policy interest rate decisions are made by the:
options: Monetary Policy Committee of the Bank of England
Financial Conduct Authority
Treasury
Office for Budget Responsibility
questions.explain: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate to meet the government's inflation target.

questions.q: An interventionist supply-side policy is:
options: Reducing trade union power
Deregulating product markets
Government spending on education and training to raise human capital
Privatising state-owned firms
questions.explain: Interventionist supply-side policies use government action, such as spending on education, training and infrastructure, to raise productive capacity.

questions.q: Which policy is an expenditure-reducing measure to correct a current-account deficit?
options: Imposing import tariffs
Deflationary fiscal policy that lowers aggregate demand
Supply-side reforms to improve competitiveness
Depreciation of the currency
questions.explain: Expenditure-reducing policies cut domestic demand (e.g. tighter fiscal/monetary policy) to reduce import spending.

questions.q: The distinction between a budget (fiscal) deficit and the national debt is that:
options: The deficit is an annual flow; the national debt is the accumulated stock of borrowing
The national debt is annual; the deficit is the total stock
The deficit only includes interest payments
They are two names for the same thing
questions.explain: A fiscal deficit is the annual excess of spending over revenue (a flow); the national debt is the total stock of accumulated government borrowing.

questions.q: Quantitative easing (QE) is best described as:
options: Increasing income tax to fund investment
The central bank creating money to buy assets, mainly government bonds, to increase the money supply
The government cutting public spending to reduce the deficit
The central bank raising the base rate to curb inflation
questions.explain: QE is an unconventional monetary policy in which the central bank purchases assets (chiefly government bonds) with newly created money to raise liquidity and lower yields.

questions.q: Export-led growth as a development strategy typically relies on:
options: exploiting comparative advantage to expand output sold abroad
fixing prices below market levels
reducing the savings ratio
raising import tariffs to protect all home industries
questions.explain: Export-led (outward-looking) growth uses trade and comparative advantage to widen markets and raise productivity.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes potential economic growth?
options: A rise in actual real GDP this year
A movement towards the PPF from inside it
An increase in the productive capacity of the economy
A fall in unemployment during a recovery
questions.explain: Potential growth is an increase in the economy's productive capacity, shown by an outward shift of the LRAS or PPF.

questions.q: The main aim of a central bank raising interest rates when the economy is overheating is to:
options: Reduce aggregate demand and inflationary pressure
Depreciate the exchange rate
Increase aggregate demand
Raise the budget deficit
questions.explain: Higher rates dampen borrowing and spending, reducing AD and easing demand-pull inflation when the economy is above capacity.

questions.q: A cut in interest rates is most likely to cause the exchange rate to:
options: Remain completely unchanged
Become fixed against the dollar
Appreciate as hot money flows in
Depreciate as the return on domestic financial assets falls and capital flows out
questions.explain: Lower interest rates reduce the relative return on domestic assets, encouraging capital outflows and tending to depreciate the currency.

questions.q: The J-curve effect describes how, following a currency depreciation, the trade balance:
options: improves immediately and then worsens
worsens at first before improving as quantities adjust
moves only if the exchange rate is fixed
remains constant throughout
questions.explain: In the short run demand is inelastic so the trade balance worsens; as volumes respond over time it improves, tracing a J shape.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and:
options: the Gini coefficient
the current-account balance
the unemployment rate
gross national income per capita (PPP)
questions.explain: HDI is a composite of life expectancy at birth, mean/expected years of schooling and GNI per head at PPP.

questions.q: Country X can produce both wheat and cloth using fewer resources than Country Y. According to comparative advantage, mutually beneficial trade is still possible provided:
options: the opportunity-cost ratios of the two goods differ between the countries
Country X has a balance-of-payments surplus
both countries fix their exchange rates
Country Y subsidises its exports
questions.explain: Gains from trade arise whenever opportunity-cost (and hence relative-cost) ratios differ, even if one country has absolute advantage in both goods.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a regressive tax?
options: A tax only paid by firms
A tax that takes a larger proportion of income from lower earners
A tax with the same average and marginal rate
A tax that takes a larger proportion of income from higher earners
questions.explain: A regressive tax, such as some indirect taxes, takes a higher proportion of income from those on lower incomes.

questions.q: Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment is most associated with:
options: A boom in the trade cycle
Workers refusing low wages
A recession when aggregate demand falls
Improvements in technology
questions.explain: Cyclical unemployment rises during recessions as a fall in aggregate demand reduces firms' need for labour.

questions.q: Real GDP is preferred to nominal GDP as a measure of growth because real GDP:
options: Counts only government output
Includes the value of the black economy
Is adjusted for inflation/changes in the price level
Is always larger than nominal GDP
questions.explain: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, allowing genuine changes in the volume of output to be measured.

questions.q: The Laffer curve suggests that beyond a certain tax rate:
options: Tax revenue is unaffected by the tax rate
Tax revenue continues to rise as rates rise
Higher tax rates reduce total tax revenue because of disincentive effects
Lower tax rates always reduce revenue
questions.explain: The Laffer curve implies that above an optimal rate, raising taxes reduces revenue as it discourages work, investment and encourages avoidance.

questions.q: An increase in the rate of saving by households, other things equal, will:
options: Have no effect on national income
Raise aggregate demand directly
Increase a withdrawal from the circular flow
Increase injections into the circular flow
questions.explain: Saving is a withdrawal (leakage) from the circular flow, so higher saving reduces the flow of income unless matched by higher injections.

questions.q: A principal role of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) is to:
options: set the value of members' exchange rates
oversee multilateral trade agreements and adjudicate trade disputes
fix world commodity prices
provide development loans to low-income countries
questions.explain: The WTO administers trade rules, promotes liberalisation and resolves disputes between members; lending and exchange rates fall to other bodies.

questions.q: A potential drawback of globalisation for a developed economy is:
options: greater access to global capital
wider consumer choice
lower prices for imported consumer goods
structural unemployment as production shifts to lower-cost economies
questions.explain: Globalisation can cause structural unemployment in higher-cost economies as labour-intensive production relocates abroad.

questions.q: The expectations-augmented (long-run) Phillips curve suggests that in the long run:
options: Higher inflation always lowers unemployment permanently
There is a permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment
The Phillips curve is downward sloping forever
Unemployment returns to its natural rate regardless of the inflation rate
questions.explain: In the long run the economy returns to the natural rate of unemployment, so the long-run Phillips curve is vertical with no permanent trade-off.

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy involves:
options: Increased government spending and/or lower taxation
Higher interest rates set by the central bank
The central bank selling government bonds
Cutting government spending to reduce the deficit
questions.explain: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government spending and/or cuts taxes to boost aggregate demand.

questions.q: A government running a balanced budget means that:
options: Tax revenue exceeds government spending
Government spending exceeds tax revenue
The national debt is zero
Government spending equals tax revenue
questions.explain: A balanced budget occurs when government spending equals tax revenue, so there is neither a deficit nor a surplus in that period.

questions.q: Automatic stabilisers refer to:
options: One-off government bailouts of banks
Central bank interventions in the foreign exchange market
Deliberate changes in tax rates announced in the Budget
Features such as progressive taxes and welfare benefits that dampen the cycle without policy changes
questions.explain: Automatic stabilisers, like progressive taxation and unemployment benefits, automatically moderate fluctuations in AD over the cycle without new policy decisions.

questions.q: The Claimant Count measure of unemployment counts:
options: People claiming unemployment-related benefits such as Jobseeker's Allowance/Universal Credit
Everyone of working age without a job
Those actively seeking work in a survey of households
Only those unemployed for over a year
questions.explain: The Claimant Count records people claiming unemployment-related benefits, whereas the ILO/Labour Force Survey measure uses a survey-based definition.

questions.q: A country has a comparative advantage in producing a good when it can produce that good at a lower:
options: level of total factor productivity
opportunity cost than its trading partner
monetary price using domestic currency
absolute quantity than its trading partner
questions.explain: Comparative advantage rests on the lower opportunity cost of production, not on absolute output or price.

questions.q: Discretionary fiscal policy differs from automatic stabilisers because it involves:
options: Changes in the exchange rate
Only the actions of the central bank
Deliberate, active changes to spending or taxation by the government
No change in government policy
questions.explain: Discretionary fiscal policy involves deliberate decisions to alter spending or taxes, unlike automatic stabilisers which operate without new decisions.

questions.q: The monetary transmission mechanism describes how:
options: Banks create money through lending
Productivity growth raises potential output
Tax changes feed through to government revenue
A change in interest rates affects AD through channels such as borrowing, saving, asset prices and the exchange rate
questions.explain: The transmission mechanism is the process by which a change in the policy rate influences spending and inflation via borrowing costs, asset prices, confidence and the exchange rate.

questions.q: A positive output gap exists when:
options: Actual output exceeds the productive potential of the economy
Actual output is below the trend rate of potential output
The economy is in a deep recession
Actual output is equal to potential output
questions.explain: A positive output gap occurs when actual real output is above the long-run potential output, typically generating inflationary pressure.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-tariff barrier to trade?
options: A floating exchange rate
A specific per-unit tax on imports
Strict domestic technical and safety standards applied to imports
An ad valorem import duty
questions.explain: Non-tariff barriers include regulations, standards and administrative rules that restrict imports without using a formal tariff.

questions.q: One supply-side benefit claimed for reducing the power of trade unions is that it may:
options: Raise the natural rate of unemployment
Increase cost-push inflation
Reduce the size of the workforce
Improve labour market flexibility and reduce structural unemployment
questions.explain: Reducing union power is argued to increase wage flexibility and labour mobility, lowering frictional and structural unemployment.
